summary: OAuth access tokens are often bearer tokens, meaning anyone who steals one can use it. DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) has the client prove at the application level that it holds a particular key each time it uses a token. This makes stolen access and refresh tokens much harder to replay.

plainLanguage.summary: A movie ticket that anyone can use is risky if you drop it. DPoP is like also showing a secret handshake only you know, so a stranger holding your ticket can't get in.

questions: how to prevent oauth token replay
how does dpop prevent token theft
subtitle: How an OAuth client proves, on every request, that it holds the private key a token was issued to, so stolen tokens are not enough.

tldr.problem: Typical bearer tokens can be used by anyone who holds them, so a leaked or stolen access or refresh token can be replayed by an attacker.
tldr.mechanism: The client signs a small JWT, the DPoP proof, with its own private key and sends it in a DPoP header on each request. The authorization server binds tokens to the matching public key, and servers check the proof against that key.
tldr.outcome: A stolen token alone becomes unusable without the private key, though DPoP does not stop an attacker who can run code inside the client or replace TLS.

today: RFC 9449 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Sender-Constrain Tokens
sections.content:
The primary aim of DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) is to prevent unauthorized parties from using leaked or stolen access tokens. A token is bound to a public key when it is issued, and the client must prove possession of the matching private key when using it. This contrasts with a typical bearer token, which any party holding it can use.

The text notes that tokens have leaked through bugs at other layers of the stack, naming CRIME, BREACH, Heartbleed and the Cloudflare parser bug, and through token theft attacks on OAuth implementations. DPoP is a defense in depth, not a substitute for secure transport, and it MUST always be used with HTTPS.

It targets cases where TLS-based binding such as RFC 8705 or token binding is not available or desirable, for example a single-page application running in a browser. DPoP can sender-constrain access tokens whatever the client authentication method, and refresh tokens issued to public clients, but it is not itself client authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: If your house key can be copied by anyone who finds it, that is risky. DPoP makes the door also ask you to prove you own the special key, not just carry a copy of a note.

sections.title: The Basic DPoP Flow
sections.content:
The main new data structure is the DPoP proof, a JWT sent in an HTTP header. Roughly, it is a signature over some data of the HTTP request, a timestamp, a unique identifier, an optional server-provided nonce, and a hash of the access token when one is present.

  1. The client sends a token request with a DPoP proof to the authorization server.
  2. The authorization server binds the access token to the public key in the proof and returns it with token_type DPoP. A refresh token issued to a public client is bound to that key too.
  3. To use the token, the client sends it with a fresh DPoP proof for that request to the resource server.
  4. The resource server checks the proof signature and claims, that the token's bound key matches the proof key, and that the token hash matches. It refuses the request if any check fails.

The resource server learns the bound key either from the access token itself (for JWT access tokens) or through token introspection.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your secret handshake to get a ticket, and the ticket is stamped with your handshake. Every time you use it, you do the handshake again.

sections.title: DPoP Proof JWTs
sections.content:
The proof is sent in the DPoP HTTP header, and each HTTP request requires a unique proof. It is signed with a private key chosen by the client. The JOSE header MUST contain typ with the value dpop+jwt, alg naming an asymmetric signature algorithm (never none or a symmetric one), and jwk holding the public key and no private key.

The payload MUST contain jti (a unique identifier, for example at least 96 bits of pseudorandom data or a version 4 UUID), htm (the HTTP method), htu (the target URI without query and fragment) and iat (creation time). On protected resource access it MUST also contain ath, the base64url SHA-256 hash of the access token. If a server supplied a nonce it MUST contain nonce.

Only the method and URI of the request are covered. This keeps the design simple by avoiding the difficulty of normalizing whole HTTP messages.

A server validating a proof checks, among other things, that there is only one DPoP header, the JWT is well formed, typ and alg are acceptable, the signature verifies with the jwk key, htm and htu match the request, any nonce matches, and the creation time is in an acceptable window. At a resource server it also checks ath and the key binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proof is a note you sign fresh for one request. It says which door you are knocking on, what you are doing, and when, and it carries your public stamp so the guard can check your signature.

sections.title: Getting and Using Bound Tokens
sections.content:
To request a bound token, the client MUST send a valid DPoP proof in the DPoP header of the access token request, for any grant type. If the proof is invalid the authorization server returns an error with invalid_dpop_proof. On success the response carries token_type DPoP. An authorization server MAY instead issue non-bound access tokens with token_type Bearer, which for a public client still binds the refresh token. Refresh tokens issued to confidential clients are not bound to the DPoP key because they are already sender-constrained by client authentication.

The resource server must be able to tell that a token is bound. The binding is carried in a cnf claim with a jkt member, the base64url SHA-256 JWK Thumbprint of the DPoP public key, or is returned in a token introspection response.

The token is sent in the Authorization header with the DPoP scheme, alongside the DPoP proof header. The resource server MUST NOT grant access unless all checks pass. A resource that supports both schemes MUST reject a DPoP-bound token presented as a bearer token. Failures use a 401 response with a WWW-Authenticate: DPoP challenge, which can carry algs, error, invalid_dpop_proof or use_dpop_nonce.

Authorization servers can advertise support with dpop_signing_alg_values_supported, and clients can be registered with dpop_bound_access_tokens so the server rejects their token requests lacking a proof.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket office stamps your ticket with your handshake. At the door, you hand over the ticket and do the handshake, and the guard checks both match.

sections.title: Server-Provided Nonces and Code Binding
sections.content:
Without more, someone controlling the client could create proofs for use arbitrarily far in the future by choosing the iat value. To limit this, an authorization server MAY require a server-chosen, unpredictable nonce in the proof. It answers a request without one with an HTTP 400 error use_dpop_nonce and a DPoP-Nonce header, and the client retries with the nonce in the nonce claim. Servers can send a fresh nonce in a later error or in a 200 OK response, which saves a round trip. Resource servers can do the same with a 401 response. Nonces from different servers must not be mixed up, and a nonce only works at the server that issued it.

The RFC also lets the authorization code be bound to the DPoP key. A client may add the dpop_jkt parameter, the JWK Thumbprint of its key, to the authorization request, and the server rejects the token request unless the proof key matches. With Pushed Authorization Requests, either dpop_jkt or a DPoP header on the pushed request can carry the key, and servers supporting both PAR and DPoP MUST support both.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard sometimes calls out a random word that you must write on your note. That way you cannot prepare notes far in advance and hand them to someone else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A captured proof can be replayed at the same endpoint, so servers MUST accept proofs only for a limited time after creation, preferably seconds or minutes. They can also store each jti for that window and reject repeats, though that may not be feasible when servers share no state. The ath claim limits pre-generated proofs to the lifetime of the access token, and deployments without nonces SHOULD NOT issue long-lived DPoP-bound access tokens. A server MUST NOT accept proofs without the nonce claim once it has given the client a nonce.

If an attacker can run code in the client, for instance through cross-site scripting, DPoP's security is no longer guaranteed. A non-exportable key stops the key being stolen, but the attacker can still create proofs while the client is online. Servers MUST verify that typ is dpop+jwt and MUST NOT allow the none algorithm.

DPoP does not protect the integrity of the request body or most headers, since the proof covers only method and URI. The RFC calls this an intentional design decision and relies on TLS in many setups. All the hashes (jkt, ath, dpop_jkt) use SHA-256 on purpose, and a short update specification is expected if another hash is ever needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret handshake only helps if nobody sneaky is standing inside your house. If they are, they can do the handshake for you, so you still must keep your house safe.

sections.title: What Was Registered
sections.content:
IANA registered the DPoP access token type and HTTP authentication scheme, the error values invalid_dpop_proof and use_dpop_nonce, and the dpop_jkt authorization request parameter. It registered the JWT claims htm, htu and ath, the jkt confirmation method, and the HTTP header fields DPoP and DPoP-Nonce.

It also registered the application/dpop+jwt media type, the metadata names dpop_signing_alg_values_supported and dpop_bound_access_tokens, and expanded the registered description of the nonce claim so it can apply beyond its original context.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name list got new entries so everyone uses the same words for the headers and settings DPoP needs.
